opening.headline: After setting delay targets, we learn how to distinguish which methods reduce delays in specific segments.
body: When users complain about slow responses, they typically start by switching models or reducing the prompt length. However, when these approaches fail to help, they repeatedly try other methods without knowing where the delay actually originates.

This lecture divides the components into delay input processing, first token, and remaining token generation, and distinguishes how model selection, input reduction, streaming, and parallelization operate in each phase. Finally, it follows the process of breaking down goals and applying methods using a consultation chatbot that takes eight seconds as a case study.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the relationship between delay time objectives and means.
Model selection, caching, streaming, and parallelization effects can be distinguished.

screens.title: The goal has been defined, but it's unclear where to reduce.
screens.lead: First, let's examine the typical characteristics of the team responsible for handling delay issues. Watch the scene and think about where the length gets blocked.

visual.alt: A delayed target number and four distinct means cards scattered without arrows.
labels: It is unknown which means reduces which interval.

paragraphs: A team set a response time goal of "within 3 seconds" for their consultation chatbot. However, the actual response exceeds this goal, and the team cannot agree on what steps to take next. One person suggests switching from the largest model to a smaller one, while another proposes reducing the prompt size.

First, one approach is applied; if it proves ineffective, another method is tried. This happens because the delay goal is defined by a single number. With just a single number, we cannot determine which method will be effective against that number.

Latency is not a single monolithic entity but rather a sum of multiple components. The time to process input, the time until the first token is generated, and the time to generate the remaining tokens each occupy distinct portions. The question posed in this lesson is how to decompose latency so that it can be tied to specific components.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When does the user feel they are waiting? Is it when the entire response is complete, or when the first character appears? You will be able to answer this question again when the lesson concludes.

screens.outro: Now let's recall how latency targets are determined in your service.

screens.title: Recall the latency target of our service
screens.lead: First think through each question mentally, then select an answer. Do not enter or submit an answer; instead, the instructor's thought process will be presented.

items.prompt: If there's a latency target, where did that number come from? Was it based on user expectations, contractual agreements, or competitive services?
items.answer: When the rationale behind the goal is clear, the criteria for selecting the means also become clear. Without a solid basis, it is difficult to determine whether a given numerical target has been achieved, regardless of the effectiveness of the means employed. Establishing the rationale for setting the goal should be the starting point.

items.prompt: Is what the user sees the total completion time, or the time when the first character appears?
items.answer: In chat-based services, the time when the first character appears has a greater impact on user perception than the time when the response ends. Conversely, in automated processes where the full result is required, completion time is more important. The desired outcome shape varies depending on the service usage pattern.

items.prompt: What becomes frustrating when the goal is not achieved?
items.answer: The strictness of the goal varies depending on whether the user is dropping off, whether the next step is delayed, or whether contractual thresholds are exceeded. By understanding the type of inconvenience, one can focus on only the essential segments rather than attempting to reduce all segments.

screens.outro: Based on these questions, I will verify diagrammatically how delay is divided into various components.

screens.title: Delay is the sum of multiple components.
screens.lead: Select the numbered marker attached to the diagram to view the meaning of each section and its representative mitigation measures. Please check them in sequence from number 1.

visual.alt: A horizontal timeline divided into input processing, first token, and remaining generation phases, from request transmission to response completion.

markers.label: Input processing
markers.title: Input processing section
markers.body: The longer the prompt, the more input tokens the model must read. OpenAI's delay optimization guide explains that reducing input is typically not a major factor. Even when the prompt is halved, delay improvement may only amount to 1–5%. This only becomes significant when the input is extremely large, such as with documents or images.

markers.label: first token
markers.title: Time until the first token
markers.body: The Claude document refers to this phase as time to first token, or abbreviated TTFT. It is the time elapsed from when the prompt is sent until the first token is generated. This metric is particularly important when using streaming. The moment a user sees the first character is determined by TTFT.

markers.label: Remaining generation
markers.title: The remaining token generation segment
markers.body: OpenAI's guide explains that token generation is almost always the most delayed stage. An empirical rule is that reducing the output tokens by half roughly cuts the delay in half. Requesting a shorter answer or setting an upper limit of `max_tokens` has an effect in this phase.

markers.label: Model speed
markers.title: Token processing speed
markers.body: The factor determining the overall length of the rod is the model's token processing speed. Smaller models are generally faster and more cost-effective. The Claude documentation recommends Haiku 5.5 for use cases where speed is critical, illustrating an example of reducing `effort` to `low`. The quality of smaller models can be compensated for with more detailed prompts or few-shot examples.

markers.label: Call stage
markers.title: Call count and order
markers.body: If requests are made repeatedly, round-trip times accumulate with each call. Steps that are not strictly sequential can be sent in parallel, and steps that can be processed together can be combined into a single prompt. Conversely, steps that require the output of a preceding step cannot be sent in parallel.

screens.outro: Having verified the components, we will now compare which intervals are reduced across different methods.

screens.title: The shrinking sections vary depending on the case.
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify how the feature applies to different sections. Pay attention to whether actual latency is reduced, or only perceived latency is reduced.

tabs.label: Model Selection
tabs.body:
This is a means of increasing the speed at which tokens are processed. Smaller models are generally faster and cheaper, and OpenAI's guide notes that, when used properly, they can outperform larger models. If quality is a concern, it can be improved through more detailed prompts, few-shot examples, or fine-tuning.

This is also a means of reducing actual latency. However, since switching models may alter the quality of the responses, verification is necessary before the transition.

tabs.label: Reduce input and caching
tabs.body:
A method to reduce the number of input tokens to process. The OpenAI guide mentions approaches such as pruning search results or cleaning up HTML, and explains that placing commonly repeated prefixes at the beginning of the prompt and varying content at the end can make caching more effective.

The magnitude of improvement depends on the size of the input. Even if the prompt is halved, the improvement might only be 1–5%, so alternative methods should be considered unless the input is extremely large.

tabs.label: streaming
tabs.body:
This is a method where the model begins sending back the previously generated parts before completing the full response. The overall completion time remains almost unchanged, but users see the first character quickly. OpenAI's guide classifies this as a principle for reducing user waiting time and introduces it as one of the most effective ways to reduce wait times to under one second.

This reduces perceived latency but does not reduce actual completion time.

tabs.label: Parallelization
tabs.body:
This method sends independent calls simultaneously to reduce overall execution time. The document uses the analogy that washing two loads takes only as long as one load drying. Even when steps must follow a strict sequence, steps with nearly predetermined outcomes can be started in parallel through speculative execution.

There is a limitation: if steps are interdependent, they cannot be sent in parallel.

tabs.label: Reduce requests and calls
tabs.body:
Since each call introduces round-trip latency, you can reduce the number of calls by combining sequential steps into a single prompt and receiving the results in a JSON field. Additionally, responses that can be handled by rules can be processed without using an LLM, using pre-written messages or existing UI components.

This approach eliminates the steps themselves, thereby removing the entire time duration for that section.

screens.outro: Since we've distinguished between different categories, let's proceed with examples that reduce perceived latency.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Reducing Perceived Latency through Streaming
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. The 8-second figure for the case is assumed for illustrative purposes only.

steps.title: See case
steps.body: There is a consultation chatbot that provides lengthy responses. After a question is sent, it takes 8 seconds to complete the response, during which the user sees a blank screen. The goal is to reduce the user's perception of waiting. The team is divided between the proposal to switch models and the proposal to shorten the prompt. The instructor suggests dividing the time consideration before choosing a method.

steps.title: Step 1: Time Series Decomposition
steps.body: First, process the input for 8 seconds, dividing it into the first token and the remaining token generation. Measurement shows that most of the time is spent on generating longer responses. It appears that reducing input in this case would have little effect.

steps.title: Divide the second-stage objectives into two.
steps.body: Divide one goal of eight seconds into two parts. Make the first part visible within one second, and allow the completion time to be longer. By doing this, we can distinguish which means align with which goal.

steps.title: Step 3: Apply Streaming
steps.body: Stream the content as it is generated, appending it sequentially to the screen. The user sees the first character immediately and then subsequent characters appear as they are read. This difference between waiting and observing progress is significant, as OpenAI's guide points out.

steps.title: Step 4: Add Auxiliary Tools
steps.body: Limiting response length by a directive reduces the number of output tokens as well as completion time. Additionally, sending a simple classification call that indicates the type of question to a smaller model speeds up processing. These methods operate in separate, non-overlapping segments from streaming.

steps.title: Read results by stage distinction
steps.body: Streaming alone does not significantly reduce actual completion time. However, since the first character appears quickly, perceived waiting time is greatly reduced. By separately reporting actual delay and perceived delay, we can accurately describe how each method contributes to achieving the goal. The report should also divide these two aspects into separate sections.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the benchmarks obtained from the case study.

screens.title: Delay involves breaking down goals into smaller objectives.
screens.lead: Let's summarize the core of the lesson. Go back and re-read the initial question: when does the user first perceive waiting?

paragraphs: Delay is not a single number but a composition of components: input processing, the first token, and the remainder generation. When setting goals, it is necessary to distinguish between the time taken to reach the first token and the time taken to complete the process. These two represent different objectives and are governed by different mechanisms.

Model selection improves token processing speed, input reduction and caching reduce the amount of input processed, and streaming reduces perceived latency. Parallelization processes independent calls simultaneously, while call batching eliminates the processing stage altogether. Since each method reduces different aspects, it's difficult to evaluate effectiveness without first breaking down latency by approach.

It's also important to develop the habit of distinguishing between actual latency and perceived latency. Streaming does not reduce completion time, but it significantly reduces the user's sense of waiting. Understanding this difference enables you to accurately interpret what specific numbers mean in latency reports.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Do not define goals with a single number; instead, divide them into two parts: the first response and completion. This will establish criteria for selecting tools and also provide criteria for evaluating effectiveness.

glossary.def: This represents the upper bound or interval-based criteria for response time allowed by the service. It must be based on valid rationale to serve as a basis for selecting the appropriate means.
This is the time elapsed from when the prompt was sent until the first token is generated. This is particularly important metric in streaming scenarios.
This approach involves delivering the generated token before the response completes. The completion time is nearly identical, but perceived waiting time is reduced.
A method of executing independent calls concurrently to reduce overall execution time.
Selecting a small and fast model serves as a means to increase token processing speed.

misconceptions.fact: Streaming displays the already-created portion immediately, with the completion time being nearly identical. The reduction refers to the user's perceived waiting time.
Other components such as output length or call frequency might occupy a larger share. The delay should be analyzed and verified before changing the model.
If steps are dependent on each other, they cannot be sent in parallel. First, verify whether the output of the preceding step is required by the subsequent step.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Delay breaks down goals into smaller parts.
The time to the first token and the time to completion are aimed at different objectives.
Model selection, input reduction, streaming, and parallelization each have different reduction intervals.
You must distinguish between actual latency and perceived latency to accurately describe the effectiveness of the solution.
closing.reflectionLead: This question is intended to encourage you to think through it on your own. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the basis for my service latency target, and should I base it on first response or completion?

checks.q: We applied streaming to a chatbot that provides lengthy responses. Which of the following is the most accurate explanation for this change?
options: The time when the entire response ends is almost the same, but since the first character appears sooner, the perceived waiting time is reduced.
The number of output tokens decreases, reducing the total completion time by nearly half.
Input processing has become faster, reducing the time until the first token.
Independent calls that are executed simultaneously reduce the overall time.
checks.explain: Streaming displays the already-generated portion immediately but does not reduce the completion time. Therefore, it is classified as a means to reduce user waiting time.

wrong.1: Reducing completion time is effective when reducing the number of output tokens.
wrong.2: Reducing the time to the first token is due to the effects of input reduction or caching.
wrong.3: Concurrency is the effect of parallelization.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Let's consider the correct sequence of steps to reduce latency in a consultation chatbot that takes 8 seconds to complete.
items: Breaks down time into input processing, first token, and remainder generation.
Divides the goal into 'quick first character' and 'completion until'.
Displays the screen sequentially as it is generated in streaming.
Distinguishes and interprets how actual completion time and perceived waiting time differ from each other.
checks.explain: First, break down time to identify where delays occur, set goals accordingly, apply measures, and finally distinguish actual time from perceived time to interpret the results.
